Chapter 4: Family Ties and the Struggle for Understanding.
Have you ever noticed how family can shape every dream you have? Sometimes, they're your biggest cheerleaders. Other times, they’re the hurdles you’ve got to clear. In Coalwood, tradition clashed with change right at home—over dinner, in whispered talks, or even in the heat of an argument. For the boy at the heart of the rocket project, home was both a safe haven and a battlefield.
His father? He was a man built by the mine—by long days, hard choices, and the weight of responsibility. Everything he did, he did through the lens of duty. All he wanted was for his son to be safe, to have a reliable job, to carry on the family’s legacy. The idea of building rockets? Well, to him, it just seemed risky, maybe even a little foolish—something that could pull his boy away from real, steady work. His love was real, make no mistake, but it was tucked behind a wall of expectations and worries he rarely spoke out loud.
Now, the mother—she saw things differently. She remembered her own dreams, the ones she’d set aside as life moved on. When she looked at her son, she saw a spark, a shot at a future beyond the coal dust. Her support wasn’t loud, but it was powerful—a quiet kind of fierceness that stood steady even when doubts crept in.
Imagine being that boy, caught right in the middle. He wanted to make his dad proud, but his heart was pulled in another direction. Sometimes, working on those rockets felt like a way out. Other times, it just made the pressure at home even heavier. There were more arguments, more distance, each rocket launch driving a wedge between father and son.
Still, every now and then, something would break through. Maybe it was sharing a meal, hearing an old story, or catching a rare smile from his father. Those moments reminded him—and maybe all of us—that love isn’t always easy to spot. His mom’s quiet encouragement became his anchor, her faith in him a shield against all the disappointment swirling around.
And it wasn’t just his family. His friends faced the same uphill climb. Their parents worried too, afraid of the risks, worried about wasting time or rocking the boat. Some people saw the rocket project as a distraction; others thought it threatened the way things had always been. The boys had to figure out how to stand up for themselves, sometimes by digging in, sometimes by finding ways to connect.
As the science fair drew closer, everything was on the line. The boys threw themselves into their work, desperate to prove what they could do—not just to win a ribbon, but to show their families and their town what was possible. The pressure was real, but so was their sense of purpose.
